controversies/same-sex-relationships-deb: Should the church bless and marry same-sex couples?

Since the mid-20th century churches have debated whether the historic teaching that sex belongs only in man–woman marriage should be maintained or revised to affirm faithful same-sex partnerships. The question has divided Anglicans, Lutherans, Presbyterians and Methodists, strained Catholic and Orthodox relations with Protestants, and set Global North against Global South.

God made us male and female and joined them in marriage as a living picture of Christ and his Church. Every text of Scripture that speaks of same-sex intercourse, from Leviticus to Paul, rejects it, and Jesus himself defined marriage by Genesis. We do not hold this out of hostility: we repent where the church has shown contempt, and we want gay and lesbian brothers and sisters fully loved, befriended and included. But love cannot bless what Scripture and the whole church across the centuries call sin. Celibacy is hard, yet Christ calls all of us to costly discipleship and promises to be enough.

The Bible’s handful of prohibitions condemn exploitation and excess in a world that knew nothing of people whose orientation is lasting and who seek lifelong covenant with one partner. What Scripture honours in marriage is faithful, self-giving, one-flesh kinship, and same-sex couples can live that. When the early church saw the Spirit poured out on uncircumcised Gentiles, it changed its practice; we see the Spirit’s fruit in gay and lesbian Christians today. Demanding lifelong celibacy of them all turns a gift into a law, and the harm done by exclusion is a moral fact the church cannot ignore.

Unresolved, with divisions. Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, most evangelical, Pentecostal and Global South churches maintain the historic teaching; a number of mainline Protestant churches in the West have adopted affirming practice. The debate has produced splits (ACNA, Global Methodist Church, departures from ELCA and PC(USA)) and continuing tensions in the Anglican Communion and the Catholic Church.

controversies/contraception-debate/summa: Until 1930 every major church opposed contraception. The Anglican Lambeth Conference first permitted it for serious reasons; Protestants followed, while the Catholic Church, after a papal commission favoured change, reaffirmed the prohibition in Humanae Vitae (1968).
controversies/contraception-debate/sides: God wove love and life together in the marital act. To keep the act but deliberately sterilise it is to take apart what God joined. Couples may space children for serious reasons by respecting the body’s natural rhythms, but they may not make themselves masters of the sources of life. The fruits of the contraceptive age, in broken families and the treatment of sex as recreation, show the wisdom of the Church’s warning.
Inseparability of unitive and procreative meanings

Marital union expresses and deepens love even when no child can result, as in the infertile or elderly. God entrusts couples with responsible stewardship of their fertility. If natural family planning is legitimate, the morally decisive factor is the couple’s faithful, generous intent, not the method; contraception can serve the good of marriage and children.
controversies/contraception-debate/timel: Lambeth Resolution 15 permits contraception; Pius XI’s Casti Connubii condemns it.

controversies/contraception-debate/resol: Divergent settlements: Catholic teaching prohibits artificial contraception (widely not followed in the West); Protestants overwhelmingly accept it; many Orthodox accept non-abortifacient methods within marriage under pastoral guidance.
controversies/contraception-debate/conse: A defining Catholic–Protestant divergence in sexual ethics.

controversies/polygamy-and-baptism/quest: Must a polygamous convert put away all but one wife before baptism?
controversies/polygamy-and-baptism/title: Polygamy and baptism in African churches
controversies/polygamy-and-baptism/summa: Missionaries in Africa and elsewhere faced men with several wives who sought baptism. Most missions required them to dismiss all but one wife; critics from Bishop Colenso to African theologians argued this punished women and children and was not required by Scripture. African Initiated Churches often accepted polygamous members, and Lambeth 1988 opened a pastoral exception.
controversies/polygamy-and-baptism/sides: From creation God’s pattern is one man and one woman, and Jesus restored that pattern. Church leaders must be "the husband of one wife". To baptise polygamists would sanction a practice contrary to the gospel and undermine Christian marriage for the next generation. A convert must obey Christ even at great cost, while making just provision for the wives he releases.
Harm to dismissed wives and children
Baptise polygamous converts with their families

A man who married several wives before hearing the gospel has made binding covenants; forcing him to divorce them breaks faith, shames the women and abandons children. Scripture never commands such dismissal; the Old Testament saints were polygamous and the New Testament restricts only leaders. Baptise the family as it is, forbid further wives, and let monogamy grow as the church’s norm.
controversies/polygamy-and-baptism/timel: Colenso first raises the question after arriving in Natal; his Remarks follow in 1862.
Lambeth Conference resolves that polygamists should not be baptised but their wives may be.
William Wade Harris baptises polygamous converts in his West African mass movement.

controversies/polygamy-and-baptism/resol: Catholic and most Protestant mission churches continue to require monogamy for full communion while increasingly providing pastoral accommodation; Anglicans since 1988 allow baptism of polygamous converts with conditions; many African Initiated Churches accept polygamous members. All major traditions teach monogamy as the Christian norm for new marriages.
controversies/polygamy-and-baptism/conse: A factor in the rise of African Initiated Churches.
Debates on inculturation and African marriage customs.
controversies/is-contemplative-prayer-bi: Are contemplative and repetitive methods of prayer faithful to Scripture?
Is contemplative prayer biblical?

Silent, wordless or repetitive prayer, from the Jesus Prayer and The Cloud of Unknowing to modern Centering Prayer, has been prized by monks and mystics and rediscovered by many Protestants. Critics, from some Reformers to modern evangelicals and even a 1989 Vatican letter, warn of technique, "vain repetitions" and borrowing from non-Christian meditation. The debate turns on what biblical meditation is and how experience is tested.
Contemplative tradition

The God who speaks also invites us to be still and know him. The Desert Fathers, the Cloud of Unknowing, the Carmelites and the hesychasts all teach a prayer beyond many words, in which we simply consent to God’s loving presence. This is not an Eastern import but the deepest current of our own tradition, always joined to Scripture, sacraments and charity, and it heals the anxious, distracted self that modern life produces.
Psalm 46:10 and 1 Kings 19:12 (the still small voice)
Romans 8:26: the Spirit prays beyond words

Biblical prayer is a conversation with a personal God, grounded in his promises: the Psalms are full of words, arguments and petitions. Jesus warned against empty repetitions. Biblical meditation fills the mind with Scripture; it does not empty it. When Christians adopt methods designed to still the mind or seek altered states, they risk confusing psychological experience with the Spirit and blurring the line between Creator and creature.

The Jesus Prayer is not a mantra but the tax collector’s cry addressed to a Person, prayed in humility within the Church’s life and under a spiritual father. Its repetition is like a child calling its mother, not heathen babbling; and its goal is not an empty mind but a heart filled with Christ.

Contemplative prayer is officially affirmed in Catholic and Orthodox teaching, with cautions about methods and guidance. Among Protestants it is widely practised in mainline and many evangelical churches, but strongly opposed by some Reformed and fundamentalist writers. No common resolution exists.
